theory.intro: The graphs of $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$ and $y=\tan x$ all fail the horizontal line test, so none of them has an inverse function. **Restricting the domain** means keeping only a piece of the curve on which the function is one-to-one.
facts: For each height in $[-1,1]$, a horizontal line meets $y=\sin x$ infinitely often, so infinitely many $x$-values share that $y$-value. Horizontal lines at heights outside $[-1,1]$ have no intersections.

A restricted piece must be one-to-one to have an inverse function. To obtain an inverse whose domain is the original function's full range, the piece must also take every value in that range; a one-to-one piece with a smaller range still has an inverse function.
The agreed restriction for sine is $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, where sine increases steadily from $-1$ to $1$.
The agreed restriction for cosine is $0\le x\le\pi$, where cosine decreases steadily from $1$ to $-1$.
The agreed restriction for tangent is $-\frac{\pi}{2}<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$, an open interval because $\tan x$ is undefined at $\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
steps: Check the function is defined everywhere on the interval
Check no horizontal line meets the curve more than once on the interval
If the inverse must have the original function's full range as its domain, check the piece still takes every value in that range

workedExamples.question_text: Explain why $y=\cos x$ has no inverse function on its natural domain.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The horizontal line $y=\frac12$ meets the curve at both $x=-\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$.
Different inputs give the same output, so cosine is not one-to-one. Its inverse relation is therefore not a function.

workedExamples.question_text: State the agreed domain restrictions used to define the inverses of sine, cosine and tangent. Explain which endpoints are included.
workedExamples.solution_text:
For sine, use $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Sine increases from $-1$ to $1$ on this interval.
For cosine, use $[0,\pi]$. Cosine decreases from $1$ to $-1$ on this interval.
Both functions are defined at their endpoints, so square brackets include them.
For tangent, use $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Tangent increases on this branch, but is undefined at both endpoints. Round brackets exclude them.

workedExamples.question_text:
Decide whether each proposed restriction gives an inverse function. Where it does, decide whether the inverse has domain $[-1,1]$.
(a) $y=\sin x$ on $[-\pi,0]$.
(b) $y=\cos x$ on $[-\pi,0]$.
(c) $y=\sin x$ on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},0\right]$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sin\left(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=-\frac12$.
Both inputs lie in the interval. A horizontal line meets the piece twice, so it has no inverse function.
(b) Cosine increases steadily from $\cos(-\pi)=-1$ to $\cos0=1$. The piece is one-to-one and takes every value in $[-1,1]$, so its inverse exists and has domain $[-1,1]$.
(c) Sine increases steadily from $-1$ to $0$, so the piece has an inverse function. Its range is only $[-1,0]$, so the inverse has domain $[-1,0]$, rather than $[-1,1]$.

workedExamples.question_text: For $f(x)=\sin x$ on $0\le x\le4\pi$, find the largest interval containing $x=3\pi$ on which an inverse function exists. Justify your answer.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The neighbouring turning points are at $x=\frac{5\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{7\pi}{2}$.
Between them, sine decreases steadily from $1$ to $-1$, so the piece is one-to-one. Both endpoints are included because sine is defined there.
Extending past either turning point repeats values. The largest interval is $\left[\frac{5\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{2}\right]$.

The branch lies between the vertical asymptotes at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$. Tangent is undefined at both endpoints, so the domain is $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.
The curve increases steadily throughout this interval. No horizontal line meets it twice, so the restricted function has an inverse.

workedExamples.question_text: A student proposes restricting $y=\tan x$ to $[-\pi,0]$. Give two separate reasons why this fails.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Tangent is undefined at $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$, which lies inside the proposed interval.
Also, $\tan(-\pi)=\tan0=0$, so different inputs in the interval give the same output. The piece is not one-to-one.

foundation.question_text: Explain why $y=\sin x$ has no inverse function on its natural domain.
foundation.solution_text:
A horizontal line such as $y=\frac{1}{2}$ cuts $y=\sin x$ infinitely many times.
So $y=\sin x$ fails the horizontal line test and is not one-to-one.
A function only has an inverse function when it is one-to-one, so $y=\sin x$ has no inverse function until its domain is restricted.

foundation.question_text: State the agreed restricted domain used to define the inverse of $y=\sin x$.
State the agreed restricted domain used to define the inverse of $y=\cos x$.
State the agreed restricted domain used to define the inverse of $y=\tan x$, and say why the endpoints are excluded.
foundation.solution_text:
$-\frac{\pi}{2}<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$
The endpoints are excluded because $\tan x$ is undefined at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, where the graph has vertical asymptotes.

foundation.question_text: For $f(x)=\cos x$ on $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, find the largest interval containing $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$ on which the inverse function exists.
foundation.solution_text:
On $0\le x\le\pi$, cosine decreases steadily from $1$ to $-1$, so it is one-to-one.
This interval contains $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$.
Extending it to the left of $0$ repeats cosine values, and it cannot extend beyond the supplied endpoint $\pi$.
The largest interval is $[0,\pi]$.

foundation.question_text:
Is $0\le x\le\pi$ a suitable restricted domain for $y=\sin x$?
Justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
1. **Check the function is defined everywhere on the interval**
$\sin x$ is defined for all $x$, so this is satisfied.
2. **Check no horizontal line meets the curve more than once on the interval**
$\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$, and both values lie in $0\le x\le\pi$.
No, it is not suitable: the piece is not one-to-one.

development.question_text:
Is $\pi\le x\le 2\pi$ a suitable restricted domain for $y=\cos x$?
Justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
1. **Check the function is defined everywhere on the interval**
$\cos x$ is defined for all $x$.
2. **Check no horizontal line meets the curve more than once on the interval**
On $\pi\le x\le 2\pi$ the cosine curve rises steadily, so it is one-to-one.
3. **If the inverse must have the original function's full range as its domain, check the piece still takes every value in that range**
It runs from $\cos\pi=-1$ up to $\cos 2\pi=1$, covering all of $[-1,1]$.
Yes, it is suitable, although the agreed restriction is $0\le x\le\pi$.

development.question_text:
Is $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$ a suitable restricted domain for $y=\cos x$?
Justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
$\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$
Both $x$-values lie in the interval, so the horizontal line $y=\frac{1}{2}$ cuts the piece twice.
No, it is not suitable: cosine is even, so this interval is not one-to-one.

The thick section runs between the asymptotes at $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Those two values are not included, because $\tan x$ is undefined there.
$\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$

development.question_text: For $f(x)=\cos x$ on $0\le x\le4\pi$, find the largest interval containing $x=\frac{5\pi}{2}$ on which the inverse function exists.
development.solution_text:
The point $x=\frac{5\pi}{2}$ lies between the turning points at $x=2\pi$ and $x=3\pi$.
On $2\pi\le x\le3\pi$, cosine decreases steadily from $1$ to $-1$, so it is one-to-one.
Extending the interval past either turning point repeats values.
The largest interval is $[2\pi,3\pi]$.

development.question_text: Why is the restricted domain of $y=\tan x$ written with round brackets, while the restricted domain of $y=\sin x$ is written with square brackets?
development.solution_text:
$\sin x$ is defined at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, taking the values $-1$ and $1$, so those endpoints are included.
$\tan x$ is undefined at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, where the graph has vertical asymptotes, so those endpoints must be excluded.
Round brackets show an excluded endpoint and square brackets show an included one.

development.question_text:
Is $0\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$ a suitable restricted domain for $y=\sin x$ if the inverse must have domain $[-1,1]$?
Justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
2. **Check no horizontal line meets the curve more than once on the interval**
On $0\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$ the sine curve rises steadily, so it is one-to-one.
3. **If the inverse must have the original function's full range as its domain, check the piece still takes every value in that range**
It runs only from $\sin 0=0$ to $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$, so it takes no negative values.
No, it is not suitable for the stated requirement: the piece misses every value in $-1\le y<0$.
It does have an inverse function, but that inverse has domain $[0,1]$.

mastery.question_text:
Give a restricted domain for $y=\sin x$, different from the agreed one, on which sine is one-to-one and still takes every value from $-1$ to $1$.
Justify your choice.
mastery.solution_text:
Choose $\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{3\pi}{2}$.
On this interval the sine curve falls steadily from $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$ to $\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-1$, so no horizontal line cuts it twice.
Because it runs from $1$ down to $-1$, it takes every value in $[-1,1]$.

mastery.question_text:
A student claims that $y=\tan x$ can be restricted to $0\le x\le\pi$ to obtain an inverse function.
Give two separate reasons why this fails.
mastery.solution_text:
First, $\tan x$ is undefined at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, which lies inside the interval, so the function is not defined on the whole interval.
Second, $\tan 0=0$ and $\tan\pi=0$, so the horizontal line $y=0$ cuts the graph twice on $0\le x\le\pi$ and the piece is not one-to-one.
Either reason on its own is enough to rule the interval out.

mastery.question_text:
For $f(x)=\sin x$ on $0\le x\le4\pi$, find the largest interval containing $x=2\pi$ on which the inverse function exists.
Justify your answer.
mastery.solution_text:
The turning points on either side of $x=2\pi$ are at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi}{2}$.
On $\frac{3\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{5\pi}{2}$, sine increases steadily from $-1$ to $1$, so it is one-to-one.
Both turning points are included because sine is defined there.
Extending the interval beyond either turning point repeats values.
The largest interval is $\left[\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{2}\right]$.
